Although this question has been hotly debated among researchers for decades, the answers yielded so far are ambiguous and inconclusive. The paper proposes an innovative approach that takes not only interregional differences in unemployment rates, but also in unemployment duration and the human capital of the unemployed, that is, in the structure of regional unemployment into account. Both, the skill structure of the unemployed and the share of long‐term unemployment are found to have an important impact on regional start‐up activity. Moreover, the impact of unemployment structure on new firm formation is found to vary with the knowledge‐intensity of the start‐ups. Introduction Scholars have devoted considerable attention to unravelling the relationship between unemployment and entrepreneurship, or the start‐up of new businesses. On the one hand, the model of entrepreneurial choice prevalent in the labour economics literature suggests that higher levels of unemployment will induce more people to making the decision to enter into entrepreneurship (Taylor 1996; Parker 2009). According to Blau (1987), Evans and Jovanovic (1989), Evans and Leighton (1990) and Blanchflower and Meyer (1994), the opportunity cost of starting a new business decreases as the likelihood of unemployment increases. Hence, according to this view, higher rates of unemployment push people into making a choice for entrepreneurship due to a lack of employment opportunities.17 On the other hand, a very different but also massive literature in regional economics has argued that entrepreneurial opportunities are less prevalent in regions with higher unemployment. According to this view, lower rates of unemployment typically reflect a region characterized by higher levels of demand and growth as well as an abundance of entrepreneurial opportunities. Such regions have a prevalence of demand‐induced entrepreneurial activities, suggesting that the pull of such opportunities triggers entrepreneurial activity (Reynolds et al. 1994, 1995; Storey 1991). Attempts to empirically unravel the relationship between entrepreneurship and unemployment have resulted in what has been characterized as ambiguity and confusion (Armington and Acs 2002; Audretsch et al. 2005). While some studies have empirically validated the push perspective, others have found empirical results consistent with the pull hypothesis (see Section 2 for a more detailed discussion). However, one aspect that studies generating these disparate results have in common is that they all treat unemployment as an unequivocal, homogeneous economic status. Such a gross characterization, treating all unemployed as being the same, flies in the face of both labour economics theory and empirical evidence. In fact, labour economics has long identified unemployed workers as consisting of very heterogeneous and disparate individuals with very different incentives and opportunities to become self‐employed (Feldstein 1973; Evans and Leighton 1990; Summers 1990). Introduction Entrepreneurs play a double role in the economy, especially in the labour market. Firstly, entrepreneurship can be treated as a form of economic activity, as opposed to the workers. According to the theory of occupational choice, everyone can choose a form of economic activity between being an entrepreneur or a paid worker. Entrepreneurs receive the entrepreneurial profits of risk; workers receive salaries without risk. In this context, choosing entrepreneurship is connected with leaving the labour market. There seems to be an empirical relationship between an increase in the entrepreneurial rate and a decrease in the employment rate. Moreover, according to the theory of a recessional push toward entrepreneurship, an unfavorable situation in the labour market can create a push towards entrepreneurship through negative motivation. In this case, an increase in the entrepreneurial rate is caused by an Journal of International Studies, Vol. 3, No 1, 2010 Aleksandra Gawea 60 INNOVATIVE APPROACHES IN LABOUR FORCE DEVELOPMENT increase in the unemployment rate. Secondly, entrepreneurs are agents who decide on the utilisation of production factors, labour and financial capital. The growth of enterprises managed by entrepreneurs is connected to their need to employ workers. In this case, a higher level of activity by entrepreneurs leads to a higher level of paid employment and a lower level of unemployment. Entrepreneurship and the labour market One well-known theory of entrepreneurship, the occupational choice theory, treats being an entrepreneur as one form of professional activity, which is an alternative to being an employee. A given individual takes a decision on becoming an entrepreneur or an employee in a rational way, using all the available information to make the most profit from the chosen form of activity. An individual becomes an entrepreneur when his subjective relative entrepreneurial profit is positive as compared with the profit from other forms of economic activity (Minniti, Bygrave 1999). Generally speaking, a given individual chooses entrepreneurship instead of working as hired labour in order to maximize their usefulness, although how to determine usefulness is a debatable question. One of the best-known determinants of occupational choice is a person's attitude towards risk. This factor was initially indicated in the model proposed by Kihlstrom and Laffont (1979) and later on developed by, among others, Banerjee and Newman (1993). Employees receive a risk-free salary as hired labour, whereas entrepreneurs obtain a profit through bearing the risk of failure. Many factors influence a person's choice of economic activity; the most important of these being entrepreneurial abilities, professional skills, attitude to risk and access to start-up capital. The push hypothesis is causal in the sense that **higher unemployment raises the incentive to start a business**. It also frames unemployment as the “least attractive of the three Knightian alternatives,” reinforcing the idea that unemployment is a pressure to act [N1-F1]. The role of labor market conditions differs sharply between the two hypotheses. For the push hypothesis, the key condition is **weakness or scarcity of labor market opportunities**. It also notes that unemployed workers are heterogeneous, and that unemployment duration and human capital structure matter [N1-F1]. It also links entrepreneurship to the availability of production factors and to market structure, implying that better labor market conditions support enterprise growth rather than forcing it [N2-F2].

This distinction matters because the push hypothesis is most relevant when the labor market is tight or when unemployment is high and alternatives are limited, while the pull hypothesis is most relevant when the labor market is slack or when unemployment is low and opportunities are more abundant [N1-F1], [N2-F2]. 1. **Direction of causality**: push says unemployment increases entrepreneurship; pull says unemployment reduces or moderates entrepreneurship [N1-F1], [N2-F2].

Together, they form a fundamental tension in the literature: unemployment can either be a driver of entrepreneurship, or a constraint on it, depending on the labor market context [N1-F1], [N2-F2].

## 1. How the push hypothesis explains unemployment’s impact

### What kind of unemployment the hypothesis focuses on
The push hypothesis focuses on **higher unemployment** and especially on situations where employment opportunities are limited. It treats unemployment as the “least attractive of the three Knightian alternatives,” meaning that when unemployment rises, the alternative to starting a business becomes less appealing [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that unemployment can lead to an increase in firm formation, and that the literature refers to this as the unemployment push, refugee, or desperation effect [N1-R2]. In other words, the push hypothesis is most relevant when unemployment is high and when workers face real labor market scarcity.

### How unemployment creates pressure to start a business
Unemployment creates pressure to start a business through several causal mechanisms. First, it reduces the **opportunity cost** of entrepreneurship: the more unemployment rises, the less attractive remaining unemployed becomes, and the more attractive starting a business appears [N1-F1]. Second, it generates **negative motivation** from labor market weakness: an unfavorable labor market can push people toward entrepreneurship because it reduces the attractiveness of paid work [N2-F2]. Third, it increases **search frictions and limited alternatives**, making it harder to find a job and thus more urgent to self-employ [N1-F1].

### Which factors are emphasized as causal mechanisms
The upstream branch emphasizes **opportunity cost**, **negative motivation**, and **labor market weakness** as the key causal mechanisms [N1-F1], [N2-F2]. It also emphasizes the role of **heterogeneous unemployed states**, such as unemployment duration and human capital structure, because not all unemployed people respond the same way [N1-F1]. In addition, the regional unemployment study notes that the effect varies with the **knowledge intensity** of start-ups, showing that firm type matters [N1-F1].

### How evidence supports or limits the hypothesis
The evidence supports the push hypothesis in showing that unemployment can increase new firm formation and that the push perspective has been empirically validated [N1-F1]. But it also limits the hypothesis by showing that results are often **ambiguous and inconclusive**, and that some studies support the pull hypothesis instead [N1-F1]. The regional unemployment study further limits it by arguing that unemployment is not homogeneous and that the effect depends on **regional structure**, **unemployment duration**, and **human capital** [N1-F1]. This means the push effect is strongest when unemployment is high and when unemployed individuals face genuine labor market constraints, but it is not uniform across all unemployment conditions [N1-F1], [N1-R4], [N3-R3].

## 2. How the pull hypothesis explains unemployment’s impact

### What kind of unemployment the hypothesis focuses on
The pull hypothesis focuses on **lower unemployment** and stronger labor markets. It treats unemployment as a condition that can reduce entrepreneurial activity because entrepreneurial opportunities are less prevalent in regions with higher unemployment [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that lower unemployment reflects economic strength, and that better labor markets can create more favorable conditions for entrepreneurship [N1-F1], [N2-R2]. In other words, the pull hypothesis is most relevant when unemployment is low and when the labor market is strong.

### How unemployment expands business opportunities or reduces barriers
Unemployment expands business opportunities or reduces barriers by improving the **labor market environment**. The evidence states that lower unemployment is associated with higher demand and growth, which can create more entrepreneurial opportunities [N1-F1]. It also notes that attractive and potentially profitable business opportunities attract individuals into entrepreneurial activity [N2-R2]. In addition, the pull literature links entrepreneurship to the availability of production factors and to market structure, implying that better labor markets support enterprise growth rather than forcing it [N2-F2].

### Which factors are emphasized as causal mechanisms
The upstream branch emphasizes **demand-side incentives**, **market structure and opportunity availability**, and **resource availability and firm growth** as the key causal mechanisms [N1-F1], [N2-R2], [N2-F2]. It also highlights the role of **institutional and structural conditions**, because the effect of unemployment depends on the broader labor market and entrepreneurial environment [N1-F1].

### How evidence supports or limits the hypothesis
The evidence supports the pull hypothesis in showing that some studies find empirical results consistent with it [N1-F1]. But it also limits the hypothesis by showing that results are often **ambiguous and inconclusive** and that the push perspective has also been validated [N1-F1]. The regional unemployment study further limits it by showing that the effect of unemployment structure varies with knowledge intensity, and that **institutional features** such as unemployment duration and human capital structure matter [N1-F1]. This means the pull effect is strongest when unemployment is low and when the labor market is strong, but it can be moderated by other structural and institutional forces [N1-F1], [N1-R4], [N3-R3].

## 3. How the two hypotheses differ

### Differences in direction of causality
The most fundamental difference is the **direction of causality**. The push hypothesis says that **higher unemployment raises entrepreneurship** because it pushes people into starting a business [N1-F1], [N1-R2]. The pull hypothesis says that **lower unemployment improves entrepreneurship** because it expands opportunities and strengthens market conditions [N1-F1], [N2-R2]. In other words, the push effect is about unemployment increasing entrepreneurship, while the pull effect is about unemployment reducing or moderating entrepreneurship.

### Differences in the role of labor market conditions
The role of labor market conditions differs sharply between the two hypotheses. For the push hypothesis, the key condition is **weakness or scarcity of labor market opportunities**. Higher unemployment is treated as a negative labor market condition that reduces the opportunity cost of starting a business and creates negative motivation to enter entrepreneurship [N1-F1], [N2-F2]. For the pull hypothesis, the key condition is **strength or abundance of labor market opportunities**. Lower unemployment is treated as a positive labor market condition that expands opportunities and supports enterprise growth [N1-F1], [N2-F2]. This distinction means the push hypothesis is most relevant in **high-unemployment environments**, while the pull hypothesis is most relevant in **low-unemployment environments**.

### Differences in policy and research implications
The policy implications are also different. The push hypothesis suggests that **policy should reduce barriers to entrepreneurship** when unemployment is high, but it also warns that generous unemployment benefits can reduce entrepreneurial initiative [N2-R1], [N7-R1]. The evidence indicates that generous unemployment compensations inhibit new business creation, especially at the beginning of the period [N7-R1]. This implies a caution: in high-unemployment settings, overly generous safety nets may weaken the push effect by reducing the urgency to start a business [N7-R1]. By contrast, the pull hypothesis suggests that **policy should support the conditions that attract entrepreneurship**, such as stable labor markets, access to resources, and growth opportunities [N2-F2]. The evidence also shows that well-designed unemployment benefits can encourage entrepreneurs to open new businesses and boost the economy [N7-R4], implying that safety nets are not inherently negative; their design matters.

Research implications are similarly different. The push hypothesis encourages studies that isolate **high-unemployment environments, heterogeneous unemployed states, and search frictions** [N1-F1], [N1-R4]. The pull hypothesis encourages studies that focus on **labor market strength, opportunity availability, and market structure** [N1-F1], [N2-F2]. The upstream heterogeneity branch adds that research should also attend to **region, sector, and institutional features**, because the effect varies with unemployment type, knowledge intensity, and policy context [N1-F1], [N5-R3], [N7-R1].

## 4. How heterogeneity and context matter

The upstream branch on heterogeneity and context shows that the relationship between unemployment and new firm formation is not uniform. Effects **vary by unemployment type**, including **unemployment duration** and **human capital structure** [N1-F1]. The evidence also suggests that effects can vary by **region, sector, or demographic group**, although the provided material is more explicit about region and firm type than about demographic groups [N1-F1], [N1-R4], [N3-R3]. The regional unemployment study is centered on **regional differences** in unemployment rates, duration, and human capital, and it finds that the impact of regional unemployment on entrepreneurship depends on the **regional structure** of unemployment [N1-F1]. A sector-level entrepreneurship paper is also referenced, indicating that the relationship may differ across industries [N3-R3].

Institutional factors also moderate the hypotheses. The unemployment benefits literature shows that generous unemployment compensations can **hinder entrepreneurial initiative** [N2-R1], [N7-R1], while well-designed unemployment benefits can also **encourage entrepreneurs** to open new businesses [N7-R4]. This means that **safety nets and policy design** can change the direction of the unemployment effect: generous benefits may reduce the push effect, whereas well-designed benefits may support the pull effect [N2-R1], [N7-R1], [N7-R4]. The historical literature on unemployment and entrepreneurship further supports the idea that the relationship is fundamentally historical and shaped by institutional and structural conditions [N6-R3].

## 5. Overall synthesis

In short, the push and pull hypotheses differ in three main ways:
1. **Direction of causality**: push says unemployment increases entrepreneurship; pull says unemployment reduces or moderates entrepreneurship [N1-F1], [N2-F2].
2. **Role of labor market conditions**: push is driven by weak labor markets and limited alternatives; pull is driven by strong labor markets and abundant opportunities [N1-F1], [N2-F2].
3. **Policy and research implications**: push suggests caution with generous benefits in high unemployment; pull suggests support for conditions that attract entrepreneurship [N2-R1], [N7-R1], [N7-R4].

The evidence provided also supports a broader conclusion: the two hypotheses are not absolute but are **context-dependent**, with institutional and structural factors often determining which mechanism dominates [N1-F1], [N5-R3], [N6-R3]. This makes the relationship between unemployment and new firm formation inherently heterogeneous and best understood as a function of unemployment type, labor market conditions, and policy design [N1-F1], [N1-R4], [N3-R3].
